content.title: About
content.content: Banana is the edible fruit of the banana plant (Musa) that grows in tropical regions worldwide. Raw banana has a soft, sweet flesh, a slightly creamy texture, and a distinctive aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bananas are botanically berries, though they are commonly called fruits.
There are over 1,000 banana varieties, but the Cavendish dominates commercial markets.
Banana plants are cultivated as “pseudostems,” where the trunk is formed from leaf bases.
Raw banana is composed of more than 20% carbohydrates, mainly sugars and starch.
Banana leaves are used in cooking and construction in many cultures.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Banana provides about 358 mg of potassium per 100 g, helping maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C has antioxidant properties and supports the immune system.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in bananas promotes healthy digestion and may help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports nervous system function and participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bananas, especially those with latex‑fruit syndrome.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Raw bananas have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Bananas are calorie‑dense and sugar‑rich; excessive intake may contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw banana is usually eaten as is, sliced into pieces, added to smoothies, oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, or used as a natural sweetener.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bananas at room temperature until they ripen. Ripe bananas keep best in the refrigerator, where they stay fresh for up to 5 days. Avoid airtight containers, which accelerate ripening.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-meat-home-rec.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and meat is a classic home‑cooked dish that combines boiled pasta, a velvety cream sauce, and sautéed meat (commonly beef, pork, or chicken). The sauce is made from cream, cheese, spices and often a touch of flour for thickness. The meal is rich in protein, carbohydrates and fat, making it a hearty lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream sauces appeared in Italian cuisine in the 19th century and quickly became a staple of home recipes.
Parmesan is traditional for the sauce, but any hard cheese can be used as a substitute.
Al dente pasta retains a lower glycemic index than fully overcooked pasta.
Adding meat boosts the dish’s nutritional value and increases iron content.
Variations may include mushrooms, spinach or tomato paste to change the flavor profile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat and cheese provide a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from pasta deliver quick energy, while the fats in cream help sustain satiety.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cream and cheese are good sources of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain pasta provide B1, B2, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑watching individuals.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large amounts of saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and processed meat often contain salt; people with hypertension should limit added salt.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream can trigger reactions in those allergic to milk proteins or intolerant to lactose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and meat. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or a pinch of black pepper. The dish is eaten with a fork and spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of cream or water to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese‑free thin crust pizza is a variation of the classic pizza that replaces traditional cheese with sauce, vegetables, and spices. The thin crust gives a crisp texture, while the lack of cheese makes it lighter and suitable for those with lactose intolerance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust originated in Naples in the 19th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Without cheese, the flavor of the tomato sauce and fresh toppings shines through.
Cheese‑free pizza is often featured in vegan menus, sometimes using plant‑based cheese alternatives.
Thin crust dough is made from simple ingredients: flour, water, yeast, salt, and olive oil.
In Italy, a cheese‑less pizza is sometimes called “pizza bianca” (white pizza), though it traditionally lacks tomato sauce.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Skipping cheese reduces saturated fat content, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: Tomatoes, peppers, mushrooms and other toppings provide vitamin C, potassium and antioxidants.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Thin crust contains less fiber than whole‑grain versions, but when made with whole‑grain flour it can aid regular bowel movements.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: The absence of dairy makes this pizza suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Lower calorie count
items.content: Compared with traditional cheese pizza, this version contains fewer calories, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Thin crust is usually wheat‑based, so it is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Tomato sauce can be salty; choose low‑sodium varieties if you need to limit salt intake.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Possible allergic reactions to tomatoes, peppers, mushrooms or other toppings.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White‑flour thin crust can raise blood sugar quickly; people with diabetes may prefer whole‑grain crusts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the pizza hot straight from the oven or cooled. Slice into wedges and serve with extra vegetable toppings, a drizzle of olive oil, or fresh herbs. Vegans can add plant‑based cheese or a nut‑based sauce for extra richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness. Freeze in bags at –18 °C for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Spanish rice with ground beef is a classic dish that combines aromatic long‑grain rice sautéed with onion, garlic and spices, and tender ground beef. It is often cooked with tomato sauce, paprika and a splash of olive oil, giving it a rich flavor and a vibrant color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in Latin American cuisine, especially in Mexico and the United States, where it is known as "Spanish rice with ground beef".
Traditionally the rice is toasted briefly before simmering to keep the grains separate.
Paprika adds the characteristic red hue and a mild heat.
Some versions include corn or black beans for extra texture and flavor.
It is commonly served as a side to tacos, burritos, or as a standalone meal.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Ground beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑rich carbs
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbohydrates that deliver sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Beef and rice contribute iron, zinc and magnesium, supporting immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: When properly cooked, the rice stays fluffy and the beef stays tender, making the meal gentle on the stomach.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using fatty ground beef or excess oil can make the dish calorie‑dense.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Some pre‑made sauces may contain gluten; check labels if you have a sensitivity.

items.title: Pathogen risk
items.content: Ground beef must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate the risk of salmonella and other bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté onion and garlic until translucent, add the ground beef and brown it. Stir in the rice, paprika and tomato sauce, pour in broth, bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer covered for 15‑20 minutes until the rice is tender. For extra texture, add corn or beans during the last 5 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then transfer to an airtight container. Refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Stew, beef, canned is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected cuts of beef slowly simmered in its own juices with spices and vegetables. Canning preserves the aroma, nutrients, and makes the dish convenient for long‑term storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned beef stew is a staple for hikers and emergency kits because of its long shelf life.
The practice of meat canning began in the 19th century and enabled armies to be fed in the field.
Typical recipes include small amounts of carrot, onion and tomato paste to enhance flavor.
Cans often contain natural preservatives such as salt and nitrites to prevent spoilage.
A sealed can of beef stew can be stored at room temperature for 3–5 years if the packaging remains intact.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is one of the best dietary sources of heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Stewed beef is abundant in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals are important for immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned products often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Nitrites and other additives can be a concern for those seeking a clean diet.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible allergic reactions to beef exist.

items.title: Thermal processing
items.content: If the can is damaged, there is a risk of bacterial growth even during storage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned beef stew can be eaten straight from the can, heated in a microwave or on the stove, added to soups, casseroles, pasta dishes, or used as a filling for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 2–3 days.
